notes.s: The small bird is told to try harder by the bird with longer legs.
notes.t: The rap line's angriest track from 2015, and the one Korean critics pointed to when they argued the group was actually writing about Korean society rather than gesturing at rebellion. The whole thing is built on a single proverb about a crow-tit and a stork, and it uses that bird to argue that effort cannot close a gap that was set at birth. Everything named in the verses was in the news that year: unpaid internships sold as passion, the generation told by newspapers how many life events it had given up, the gold spoon and dirt spoon argument about inherited wealth. The last chorus switches the taunt from of course, a stork to we are crow-tits, and turns it into an invitation to live together.
k: Everything hangs on the proverb 뱁새가 황새 따라가면 가랑이가 찢어진다: if the crow-tit chases the stork, its crotch tears open. Know your station or you will injure yourself trying to leave it, and Korean parents say it to children with a straight face. 덕에 means thanks to, normally in gratitude, so thanking the stork for the damage is where the sarcasm lives. 가랑이 is the fork of the legs and 탱탱 is stretched tight, so the body is already mid-tear in the first chorus.

금수저, gold spoon, and its counterpart 흙수저, dirt spoon, came out of a mid-2010s Korean argument that your outcome is set by what your parents had. Being born with it is the whole of the sentence. Calling that person 선생님, teacher, is the sting: the one with the inheritance is also the one entitled to lecture you about working harder.

Newspapers coined 삼포세대, the three-give-up generation, for young Koreans giving up dating, marriage and children, then inflated it to five, to seven, to N. 포 is clipped from 포기, giving up. Refusing to name the number, 몇 포, mocks the press habit of counting for them.

싹수가 노랗다, the sprout has gone yellow, means something was never going to amount to anything. The stutter lands 노력, effort, and 노랗다, yellow, on the same syllable, so the lecture about effort and the verdict that you are hopeless come out of the same mouth in the same breath.

vocab.note: 열정페이, passion pay, is unpaid or barely paid work young people are told to take because the experience is the reward
Colloquial 매일, usually with irritation attached
Transitive; 바뀌다 is for something changing by itself
Wants an object: 돈을 원해. For wanting to do something you need -고 싶다
A different 정상 means the summit of a mountain, and another means a head of state
노력하다 to make an effort; the noun carries a whole Korean moral argument about deserving your outcome

vocab.en: harping on, the same old tune
vocab.note: Originally a folk song form; now 돈 타령 is someone who will not stop going on about money
손발이 오그라들다, hands and feet curling, is how Korean says cringe

vocab.en: promise, early signs of how someone will turn out
vocab.note: Almost only appears in 싹수가 노랗다 or 싹수가 있다
실망시키다 to disappoint someone, 실망하다 to be disappointed
Used for sports events and for stocks on an exchange
공평 is fairness in how things are split; 공정 is fairness of process
A homograph with 정의 meaning definition, written with different characters
